questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: In which of the following pairs is the first compound an allylic halide and the second compound a vinylic halide?
options: A) 3-Chlorocyclohex-1-ene and 1-chlorocyclohex-1-ene
B) 4-Bromobut-1-ene and 1-bromobut-1-ene
C) 1-Bromobut-2-ene and 3-bromoprop-1-ene
D) Benzyl chloride and chlorobenzene
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify allylic halides. In an allylic halide, the halogen atom is bonded to an $sp^3$-hybridized carbon atom adjacent to a carbon-carbon double bond ($-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2-\text{X}$). In 3-chlorocyclohex-1-ene, the chlorine atom is bonded to an $sp^3$ carbon (C3) directly adjacent to the double bond between C1 and C2, making it an allylic halide.
Step 2: Identify vinylic halides. In a vinylic halide, the halogen atom is bonded directly to an $sp^2$-hybridized carbon atom of a carbon-carbon double bond ($-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{X}$). In 1-chlorocyclohex-1-ene, the chlorine is attached directly to the $sp^2$ carbon (C1) involved in the double bond, making it a vinylic halide.
Step 3: Analyze incorrect choices. In 4-bromobut-1-ene, the halogen is at C4, separated by two single bonds from the double bond (homoallylic). Benzyl chloride has the halogen on an $sp^3$ carbon bonded to an aromatic ring (benzylic halide), while chlorobenzene has the halogen on an $sp^2$ aromatic carbon (aryl halide).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: What is the correct IUPAC name of the branched haloalkane represented by the condensed formula $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}-\text{CH}(\text{Cl})-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3$?
options: A) 3-Chloro-4-methylpentane
B) 3-Chloro-2-methylpentane
C) 2-Chloro-3-ethylbutane
D) 2-Methyl-3-chloropentane
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Determine the principal carbon chain. The longest continuous chain containing the carbon bonded to chlorine has 5 carbon atoms, making the parent alkane pentane.
Step 2: Number the carbon chain from both directions. Numbering from left to right gives substituents at position 2 ($-\text{CH}_3$) and position 3 ($-\text{Cl}$). Numbering from right to left gives substituents at position 3 ($-\text{Cl}$) and position 4 ($-\text{CH}_3$). The set of locants $(2, 3)$ is lower than $(3, 4)$, so numbering is correctly done from left to right.
Step 3: Alphabetize the substituent prefixes. The prefix 'chloro' precedes 'methyl' alphabetically. Therefore, the IUPAC name is 3-chloro-2-methylpentane.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements regarding the physical properties and nature of the carbon-halogen bond in haloalkanes:
Statement I: The dipole moment of chloromethane ($\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}$) is greater than that of fluoromethane ($\text{CH}_3\text{F}$).
Statement II: Although fluorine is more electronegative than chlorine, the $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond length is significantly larger than the $\text{C}-\text{F}$ bond length, making the product of charge and distance larger for $\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}$.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer:
options: A) Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
B) Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
C) Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
D) Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Analyze Statement I. According to NCERT data, the dipole moment of chloromethane ($\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}$) is $1.860\text{ D}$, whereas that of fluoromethane ($\text{CH}_3\text{F}$) is $1.847\text{ D}$. Thus, chloromethane has a higher dipole moment than fluoromethane. Statement I is correct.
Step 2: Analyze Statement II. Dipole moment is given by $\mu = q \times d$, where $q$ is the magnitude of separated partial charge and $d$ is the bond distance. Fluorine has higher electronegativity than chlorine, resulting in a larger $q$ for $\text{C}-\text{F}$. However, the $\text{C}-\text{F}$ bond distance is very small ($139\text{ pm}$) compared to the $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond distance ($178\text{ pm}$). The significantly greater distance in $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ overcompensates for the smaller charge separation, leading to a net larger dipole moment in $\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}$. Statement II is correct.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Arrange the following isomeric butyl bromides in the decreasing order of their boiling points:
(I) 1-Bromobutane ($n$-butyl bromide)
(II) 2-Bromobutane ($sec$-butyl bromide)
(III) 1-Bromo-2-methylpropane (isobutyl bromide)
(IV) 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane ($tert$-butyl bromide)
options: A) $\text{IV} > \text{III} > \text{II} > \text{I}$
B) $\text{IV} > \text{II} > \text{III} > \text{I}$
C) $\text{I} > \text{II} > \text{III} > \text{IV}$
D) $\text{I} > \text{III} > \text{II} > \text{IV}$
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand the effect of branching on boiling points. For isomeric alkyl halides, the molecular mass is identical, so the boiling point is determined by the surface area available for intermolecular van der Waals forces. With increased branching, the molecule assumes a more spherical shape, reducing surface area and weakening van der Waals attractions, which lowers the boiling point.
Step 2: Compare the structural isomers using NCERT data: 1-Bromobutane (straight chain, primary) has b.p. $375\text{ K}$; 1-bromo-2-methylpropane (branched chain, primary) has b.p. $364\text{ K}$; 2-bromobutane (secondary) has b.p. $361\text{ K}$; and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (tertiary, most spherical) has b.p. $346\text{ K}$.
Step 3: Conclude the order: $\text{I} > \text{III} > \text{II} > \text{IV}$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements labeled as Assertion (A) and Reason (R):
Assertion (A): The melting point of $p$-dichlorobenzene is significantly higher than those of its $o$- and $m$-isomers.
Reason (R): The para-isomer possesses greater molecular symmetry, which allows its molecules to pack more closely and efficiently into the crystal lattice.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer:
options: A) Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
B) Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
C) (A) is true but (R) is false
D) (A) is false but (R) is true
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Evaluate Assertion (A). According to NCERT, the melting point of $p$-dichlorobenzene is $323\text{ K}$, which is substantially higher than that of $o$-dichlorobenzene ($256\text{ K}$) and $m$-dichlorobenzene ($249\text{ K}$), even though their boiling points are nearly identical ($448\text{ K}, 453\text{ K}, 446\text{ K}$). Thus, Assertion (A) is true.
Step 2: Evaluate Reason (R). Melting point depends heavily on crystal lattice stability. The para-isomer is symmetrical, enabling it to fit closely and pack compactly into the crystal lattice. Because of tighter crystal packing, greater energy is required to break the crystal lattice during melting. Thus, Reason (R) is true and correctly explains Assertion (A).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: Thionyl chloride ($\text{SOCl}_2$) in the presence of pyridine is considered the best synthetic reagent for preparing alkyl chlorides from primary alcohols because:
options: A) The reaction proceeds through a carbocation intermediate with complete retention of configuration
B) Both by-products ($\text{SO}_2$ and $\text{HCl}$) are gases that escape from the reaction mixture, yielding pure alkyl chloride
C) Thionyl chloride acts as a strong reducing agent that prevents alkene formation
D) It selectively reacts only with the tertiary carbon atoms in alcohols
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Write the chemical equation for the Darzens process: $\text{R}-\text{OH} + \text{SOCl}_2 \rightarrow \text{R}-\text{Cl} + \text{SO}_2\uparrow + \text{HCl}\uparrow$.
Step 2: Note the states of the by-products. Sulfur dioxide ($\text{SO}_2$) and hydrogen chloride ($\text{HCl}$) are both gaseous substances under ambient reaction conditions and bubble out of the reaction vessel.
Step 3: Conclude why it is preferred: Since the by-products escape into the atmosphere, the product alkyl chloride is obtained in practically pure form without requiring tedious column chromatography or fractional distillation.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements regarding the preparation of alkyl iodides from alcohols:
Statement I: Sulfuric acid ($\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$) cannot be used along with potassium iodide ($\text{KI}$) during the conversion of alcohols into alkyl iodides.
Statement II: Sulfuric acid is a strong oxidizing agent that oxidizes hydrogen iodide ($\text{HI}$) produced during the reaction into molecular iodine ($\text{I}_2$).
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer:
options: A) Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
B) Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
C) Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
D) Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Analyze Statement I. When attempting to prepare alkyl iodides by heating alcohols with $\text{KI}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, the desired alkyl iodide is not obtained in appreciable quantity; instead, a non-oxidizing acid like orthophosphoric acid ($95\%\text{ H}_3\text{PO}_4$) must be employed. Statement I is correct.
Step 2: Analyze Statement II. Concentrated sulfuric acid is a potent oxidizing agent. It oxidizes the generated hydrogen iodide according to the redox reaction: $2\text{HI} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{I}_2 + \text{SO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$. As a result, $\text{HI}$ is destroyed before it can perform nucleophilic displacement on the protonated alcohol. Statement II is correct.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: An unknown isomeric alcohol with molecular formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$ reacts immediately at room temperature with Lucas reagent (equimolar concentrated $\text{HCl}$ and anhydrous $\text{ZnCl}_2$) to produce an oily layer of insoluble turbidity. The alcohol is:
options: A) 2-Methylpropan-1-ol
B) Butan-1-ol
C) Butan-2-ol
D) 2-Methylpropan-2-ol
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand the diagnostic mechanism of the Lucas test. Alcohols react with concentrated $\text{HCl}$ in the presence of anhydrous $\text{ZnCl}_2$ to form insoluble alkyl chlorides, producing turbidity.
Step 2: Recall the relative rates of reaction based on alcohol class. The reaction proceeds via a carbocation intermediate. Tertiary ($3^\circ$) alcohols form stable tertiary carbocations and react immediately at room temperature. Secondary ($2^\circ$) alcohols react within $5\text{ minutes}$. Primary ($1^\circ$) alcohols do not react at room temperature and produce turbidity only upon heating.
Step 3: Identify the isomeric alcohol. 2-Methylpropan-2-ol is a tertiary alcohol ($3^\circ$), so it generates turbidity immediately. Butan-2-ol is secondary ($2^\circ$), while butan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-1-ol are primary ($1^\circ$).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: In the Finkelstein reaction, alkyl bromides or chlorides are treated with sodium iodide ($\text{NaI}$) in dry acetone to synthesize alkyl iodides. The thermodynamic driving force that shifts this reversible substitution reaction towards completion is:
options: A) The precipitation of sodium chloride or sodium bromide from dry acetone, driving the equilibrium forward by Le Chatelier's principle
B) The formation of a gaseous alkyl fluoride by-product
C) The high solubility of sodium chloride in dry acetone compared to sodium iodide
D) The oxidation of iodide to periodate by the ketone carbonyl group
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Write the chemical equation: $\text{R}-\text{X} + \text{NaI} \xrightarrow{\text{dry acetone}} \text{R}-\text{I} + \text{NaX}\downarrow$ (where $\text{X} = \text{Cl}, \text{Br}$).
Step 2: Understand the role of dry acetone. Dry acetone is a polar aprotic solvent. Due to polarization and covalent character (Fajans' rule), $\text{NaI}$ is reasonably soluble in acetone. In contrast, $\text{NaCl}$ and $\text{NaBr}$ are predominantly ionic with high lattice energies, making them insoluble in acetone.
Step 3: Relate to Le Chatelier's principle. As $\text{NaCl}$ or $\text{NaBr}$ precipitates out of the acetone solution, it is removed from the active equilibrium, continuously shifting the forward reaction toward the formation of alkyl iodide.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: Which of the following inorganic reagents is specifically designated in the Swarts reaction for preparing fluoroalkanes from alkyl chlorides or bromides?
options: A) $\text{KF}$ dissolved in glacial acetic acid
B) $\text{AgF}$, $\text{Hg}_2\text{F}_2$, $\text{CoF}_3$, or $\text{SbF}_3$
C) Aqueous $\text{HF}$ in the presence of concentrated $\text{HNO}_3$
D) $\text{NaF}$ dissolved in liquid ammonia
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Define Swarts reaction. The synthesis of alkyl fluorides is best accomplished by heating an alkyl chloride or bromide in the presence of a metallic fluoride.
Step 2: Identify valid fluorinating agents. According to NCERT Class 12 Chemistry, the specific metallic fluorides used are silver fluoride ($\text{AgF}$), mercurous fluoride ($\text{Hg}_2\text{F}_2$), cobalt trifluoride ($\text{CoF}_3$), or antimony trifluoride ($\text{SbF}_3$).
Step 3: Example reaction: $\text{CH}_3\text{Br} + \text{AgF} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{F} + \text{AgBr}\downarrow$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements regarding the addition of hydrogen halides to unsymmetrical alkenes:
Statement I: The addition of hydrogen bromide ($\text{HBr}$) to propene in the presence of benzoyl peroxide gives 1-bromopropane as the major product.
Statement II: The anti-Markovnikov peroxide effect (Kharasch effect) is equally observed during the peroxide-catalyzed addition of $\text{HCl}$ and $\text{HI}$.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer:
options: A) Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
B) Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
C) Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
D) Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Evaluate Statement I. In the presence of organic peroxides, $\text{HBr}$ adds to unsymmetrical alkenes by a free-radical mechanism to give the anti-Markovnikov product. Addition of $\text{HBr}$ to propene yields 1-bromopropane as the major product. Statement I is correct.
Step 2: Evaluate Statement II. The peroxide effect is observed only with $\text{HBr}$ and not with $\text{HCl}$ or $\text{HI}$. The $\text{H}-\text{Cl}$ bond is strong ($430.5\text{ kJ/mol}$), making its homolytic cleavage by alkoxy radicals endothermic. In the case of $\text{HI}$, the $\text{H}-\text{I}$ bond is weak ($296.8\text{ kJ/mol}$), but the generated iodine radicals are unreactive towards alkenes and instead combine with each other to form molecular $\text{I}_2$ (the addition step to the alkene is endothermic). Hence, Statement II is incorrect.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements labeled as Assertion (A) and Reason (R):
Assertion (A): Reaction of haloalkanes with potassium cyanide ($\text{KCN}$) yields alkyl cyanides as the major product, whereas reaction with silver cyanide ($\text{AgCN}$) yields alkyl isocyanides as the major product.
Reason (R): Cyanide ion is an ambident nucleophile; $\text{KCN}$ is predominantly ionic allowing carbon to attack, whereas $\text{AgCN}$ is predominantly covalent with the nitrogen lone pair available for attack.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer:
options: A) (A) is false but (R) is true
B) Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
C) (A) is true but (R) is false
D) Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Evaluate Assertion (A). Treatment of an alkyl halide with alcoholic $\text{KCN}$ yields an alkyl cyanide (nitrile, $\text{R}-\text{CN}$) as the chief product, whereas with $\text{AgCN}$, an alkyl isocyanide (carbylamine, $\text{R}-\text{NC}$) is formed as the chief product. Assertion (A) is true.
Step 2: Evaluate Reason (R). The cyanide group has two nucleophilic centers (carbon and nitrogen), making it an ambident nucleophile. $\text{KCN}$ is predominantly ionic and dissociates into $\text{K}^+$ and $\text{CN}^-$. Because the $\text{C}-\text{C}$ bond ($347\text{ kJ/mol}$) is more stable and stronger than the $\text{C}-\text{N}$ bond ($305\text{ kJ/mol}$), attack occurs primarily through carbon, forming alkyl cyanide. In contrast, $\text{AgCN}$ is predominantly covalent, where silver is bonded to carbon, leaving only the unshared pair of electrons on nitrogen free to attack, leading to alkyl isocyanide. Reason (R) is true and correctly explains Assertion (A).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: What are the major organic products obtained when bromoethane is treated separately with potassium nitrite ($\text{KNO}_2$) and silver nitrite ($\text{AgNO}_2$) in ethanol, respectively?
options: A) Ethyl nitrite ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2-\text{O}-\text{N}=\text{O}$) and Nitroethane ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2-\text{NO}_2$)
B) Nitroethane ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2-\text{NO}_2$) and Ethyl nitrite ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2-\text{O}-\text{N}=\text{O}$)
C) Nitroethane in both reactions
D) Ethyl nitrite in both reactions
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Analyze reaction with $\text{KNO}_2$. Potassium nitrite is an ionic compound containing the nitrite ion ($[\text{O}-\text{N}=\text{O}]^-$). The negative charge resides on the electronegative oxygen atom. Nucleophilic attack occurs through oxygen to yield an alkyl nitrite, ethyl nitrite ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2-\text{O}-\text{N}=\text{O}$).
Step 2: Analyze reaction with $\text{AgNO}_2$. Silver nitrite is predominantly covalent with a covalent $\text{Ag}-\text{O}$ bond. The lone pair on nitrogen is available for nucleophilic attack on the carbon of the ethyl halide, producing a nitroalkane, nitroethane ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2-\text{NO}_2$).
Step 3: Conclude the respective products: ethyl nitrite with $\text{KNO}_2$, and nitroethane with $\text{AgNO}_2$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: For nucleophilic substitution reactions of haloalkanes, which of the following correctly depicts the decreasing order of leaving group ability among halide anions?
options: A) $\text{F}^- > \text{Cl}^- > \text{Br}^- > \text{I}^-$
B) $\text{I}^- > \text{Br}^- > \text{Cl}^- > \text{F}^-$
C) $\text{Cl}^- > \text{Br}^- > \text{I}^- > \text{F}^-$
D) $\text{Br}^- > \text{I}^- > \text{Cl}^- > \text{F}^-$
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Relate leaving group ability to base strength. Good leaving groups are weak bases that can comfortably accommodate the departing electron pair.
Step 2: Compare the basicity of halide ions. The acid strength of hydrogen halides decreases in the order: $\text{HI} > \text{HBr} > \text{HCl} > \text{HF}$. Thus, basicity follows the reverse order: $\text{I}^- < \text{Br}^- < \text{Cl}^- < \text{F}^-$. The weaker the conjugate base, the better the leaving group.
Step 3: Consider bond enthalpy. The $\text{C}-\text{X}$ bond strength decreases down the group: $\text{C}-\text{F} > \text{C}-\text{Cl} > \text{C}-\text{Br} > \text{C}-\text{I}$. Consequently, the leaving group ability decreases in the order: $\text{I}^- > \text{Br}^- > \text{Cl}^- > \text{F}^-$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: Which of the following statements regarding the $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ mechanism of alkyl halides is correct?
options: A) Tertiary alkyl halides react faster than primary alkyl halides due to stability of the intermediate
B) The reaction proceeds via a planar carbocation intermediate resulting in racemization
C) The reaction proceeds in a single concerted step with complete inversion of configuration (Walden inversion)
D) The rate of reaction is independent of the concentration and nature of the nucleophile
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand the concerted nature of the $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ mechanism. The bimolecular nucleophilic substitution ($\text{S}_\text{N}2$) takes place in a single step with simultaneous bond-making and bond-breaking via a pentacoordinate transition state.
Step 2: Analyze stereochemistry. The nucleophile attacks exclusively from the side opposite to the leaving group (backside attack). As the leaving group departs, the configuration of the carbon atom inverts completely, analogous to an umbrella turning inside out in a strong gale (Walden inversion).
Step 3: Contrast with incorrect statements. $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ proceeds via a carbocation and gives racemization; tertiary alkyl halides are least reactive in $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ due to steric hindrance; and the $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ rate depends on both substrate and nucleophile: $\text{Rate} = k[\text{RX}][\text{Nu}^-]$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: Which of the following features is uniquely characteristic of the unimolecular nucleophilic substitution ($\text{S}_\text{N}1$) reaction of haloalkanes?
options: A) Reactivity order of alkyl halides is $\text{CH}_3\text{X} > 1^\circ > 2^\circ > 3^\circ$
B) Second-order kinetics with rate $= k[\text{RX}][\text{Nu}^-]$
C) Strict $100\%$ inversion of configuration without any racemization
D) First-order kinetics involving a slow rate-determining ionization to form a planar carbocation intermediate
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Describe the $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ mechanism. The $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ reaction is a two-step process. Step 1 is the slow heterolysis of the $\text{C}-\text{X}$ bond to produce a planar carbocation and a halide ion. Since this step is rate-determining, the kinetics are first order: $\text{Rate} = k[\text{RX}]$.
Step 2: Understand the stereochemical consequence. The carbocation is $sp^2$-hybridized and planar. The incoming nucleophile can attack from either the front or the back face with equal probability, leading to racemization.
Step 3: Evaluate reactivity order. The reactivity order is governed by carbocation stability: $3^\circ > 2^\circ > 1^\circ > \text{CH}_3\text{X}$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: When 2-bromobutane is heated with alcoholic potassium hydroxide ($\text{alc. KOH}$), but-2-ene is formed as the major product ($81\%$) rather than but-1-ene ($19\%$). This regioselectivity is dictated by:
options: A) Zaitsev's (Saytzeff's) rule, favoring the alkene with the greater number of alkyl substituents on the double-bonded carbons
B) Hoffmann's rule, favoring the least substituted and least sterically hindered alkene
C) Markovnikov's rule, governing electrophilic addition of protic acids to alkynes
D) Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the reaction type. Heating 2-bromobutane with alcoholic $\text{KOH}$ brings about a $\beta$-elimination reaction (dehydrohalogenation).
Step 2: Apply Zaitsev's rule. Alexander Zaitsev observed that in dehydrohalogenation reactions, the preferred product is the alkene that has the greater number of alkyl groups attached to the doubly bonded carbon atoms.
Step 3: Compare product stabilities. But-2-ene ($\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_3$) is a disubstituted alkene stabilized by 6 hyperconjugative $\alpha$-hydrogens, making it thermodynamically more stable. But-1-ene ($\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$) is monosubstituted with only 2 $\alpha$-hydrogens. Hence, but-2-ene is the major product ($81\%$).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements labeled as Assertion (A) and Reason (R):
Assertion (A): Grignard reagents ($\text{RMgX}$) must be prepared in anhydrous diethyl ether and carefully protected from atmospheric moisture.
Reason (R): Grignard reagents are highly reactive bases and react vigorously with water or any compound containing active hydrogen to form hydrocarbons.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer:
options: A) Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
B) Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
C) (A) is true but (R) is false
D) (A) is false but (R) is true
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Evaluate Assertion (A). During the synthesis of Grignard reagents from haloalkanes and magnesium turnings in diethyl ether, moisture must be strictly excluded. Assertion (A) is true.
Step 2: Evaluate Reason (R). In Grignard reagents, the carbon-magnesium bond is highly polar covalent ($C^{\delta-} - \text{Mg}^{\delta+}$). The carbanion-like alkyl group acts as a powerful base and readily abstracts a proton from any active hydrogen source, such as water, alcohols, phenols, or amines: $\text{R}-\text{MgX} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{R}-\text{H} + \text{Mg(OH)X}$. This irreversibly destroys the reagent into an alkane. Thus, Reason (R) is true and correctly explains Assertion (A).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: Which of the following alkanes cannot be synthesized in good practical yield using the Wurtz reaction from a single haloalkane?
options: A) $n$-Butane
B) $n$-Hexane
C) $n$-Pentane
D) 2,3-Dimethylbutane
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand the Wurtz reaction. The reaction of an alkyl halide with sodium metal in dry ether produces a symmetrical alkane containing double the number of carbons: $2\text{R}-\text{X} + 2\text{Na} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \text{R}-\text{R} + 2\text{NaX}$.
Step 2: Analyze symmetrical vs unsymmetrical alkanes. $n$-Butane is prepared cleanly from bromoethane ($2\text{ C} \times 2 = 4\text{ C}$); $n$-hexane is prepared cleanly from 1-bromopropane ($3\text{ C} \times 2 = 6\text{ C}$); 2,3-dimethylbutane is prepared cleanly from 2-bromopropane.
Step 3: Evaluate $n$-pentane. To prepare $n$-pentane (an odd-carbon alkane, 5 carbons), a mixture of two different alkyl halides (e.g., bromoethane and 1-bromopropane) would be required. This yields a mixture of three alkanes ($n$-butane, $n$-pentane, and $n$-hexane) that have very similar boiling points and are difficult to separate, resulting in a poor yield.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Match the factors contributing to the extremely low reactivity of haloarenes towards nucleophilic substitution in List I with their descriptions in List II:
List I:
(P) Resonance effect
(Q) Hybridisation of carbon
(R) Instability of phenyl cation
(S) Electron repulsion

List II:
(1) Departure of halide without assistance creates an unstable cation where the vacant $sp^2$ orbital is perpendicular to the $\pi$ cloud
(2) Approach of an electron-rich nucleophile is impeded by the electron cloud of the aromatic ring
(3) Delocalization of halogen lone pair gives partial double bond character to the $\text{C}-\text{X}$ bond
(4) Carbon bonded to halogen is $sp^2$-hybridized with greater s-character, holding the bonding pair more tightly

Choose the correct match from the options below:
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Match (P) Resonance effect. In haloarenes, the electron lone pairs on the halogen atom are in conjugation with the $\pi$ electrons of the benzene ring, imparting partial double bond character to the $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond (bond length $169\text{ pm}$ vs $178\text{ pm}$ in chloroethane). Thus, $\text{P} \rightarrow 3$.
Step 2: Match (Q) Hybridisation of carbon. The carbon bonded to halogen in haloarenes is $sp^2$-hybridized ($33\%$ s-character), which is more electronegative and holds the bonding pair more tightly than the $sp^3$ carbon ($25\%$ s-character) in haloalkanes. Thus, $\text{Q} \rightarrow 4$.
Step 3: Match (R) Instability of phenyl cation. If the $\text{C}-\text{X}$ bond ionizes, the resulting phenyl cation has a vacant $sp^2$ orbital that cannot be stabilized by resonance because it is orthogonal to the $\pi$ system. Thus, $\text{R} \rightarrow 1$.
Step 4: Match (S) Electron repulsion. The aromatic ring is surrounded by a dense $\pi$ electron cloud that electrostatically repels incoming electron-rich nucleophiles. Thus, $\text{S} \rightarrow 2$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements regarding the electrophilic aromatic substitution reactions of chlorobenzene:
Statement I: Chlorine directs an incoming electrophile predominantly to the ortho and para positions of the benzene ring.
Statement II: Chlorobenzene reacts substantially slower than benzene in electrophilic substitutions because the inductive electron withdrawal ($-I$) of chlorine outweighs its resonance electron donation ($+R$), causing overall deactivation of the ring.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer:
options: A) Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
B) Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
C) Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
D) Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Analyze Statement I. Due to resonance ($+R$ effect), the unshared electron pairs of chlorine delocalize into the aromatic ring, resulting in a relatively higher electron density at the ortho and para positions than at the meta position. Hence, chlorine is an ortho-para director. Statement I is correct.
Step 2: Analyze Statement II. Chlorine possesses high electronegativity and exerts a strong inductive electron-withdrawing effect ($-I$). For halogens, the $-I$ effect is stronger than the $+R$ effect ($-I > +R$), leading to a net withdrawal of electron density from the benzene ring. Consequently, chlorobenzene is deactivated relative to benzene and reacts slower in electrophilic substitutions. Statement II is correct.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: Trichloromethane (chloroform, $\text{CHCl}_3$) is stored in dark brown bottles filled to the brim, and $1\%$ ethanol is added to it because:
options: A) Ethanol acts as a catalyst that accelerates the conversion of chloroform into carbon tetrachloride
B) In the presence of sunlight and atmospheric oxygen, chloroform is slowly oxidized to poisonous phosgene ($\text{COCl}_2$), and ethanol converts any formed phosgene into harmless diethyl carbonate
C) Light decomposes chloroform into chlorine gas, and ethanol precipitates chlorine as ethyl chloride
D) Chloroform reacts with amber glass to release lead, which is neutralized by ethanol
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand the oxidation of chloroform. When exposed to light and air, chloroform undergoes slow photochemical oxidation to form carbonyl chloride (phosgene, $\text{COCl}_2$), which is an extremely toxic gas: $2\text{CHCl}_3 + \text{O}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{light}} 2\text{COCl}_2 + 2\text{HCl}$.
Step 2: Purpose of dark bottles and complete filling. Dark brown bottles prevent light penetration, and filling to the brim eliminates air/oxygen contact.
Step 3: Role of 1% ethanol. Small amounts of ethanol ($1\%$) are added to suppress the oxidation and to react with any phosgene that might form, converting it into harmless, non-toxic diethyl carbonate: $\text{COCl}_2 + 2\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} \rightarrow (\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{O})_2\text{C}=\text{O} + 2\text{HCl}$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
An optically pure sample of $(R)$-2-bromooctane is subjected to hydrolysis under two distinct conditions:
Reaction 1: Treated with concentrated aqueous sodium hydroxide ($\text{NaOH}$) in acetone.
Reaction 2: Solvolysis in a $50:50$ mixture of water and ethanol without added strong base.
What are the expected stereochemical outcomes for Reaction 1 and Reaction 2, respectively?
options: A) Both Reaction 1 and Reaction 2 proceed with complete retention of configuration
B) Reaction 1 yields a racemic mixture; Reaction 2 yields $(R)$-octan-2-ol with complete retention
C) Reaction 1 yields $(S)$-octan-2-ol with complete inversion; Reaction 2 yields a racemic mixture of $(R)$- and $(S)$-octan-2-ol with slight excess of $(S)$-octan-2-ol
D) Reaction 1 yields $(R)$-octan-2-ol; Reaction 2 yields $(S)$-octan-2-ol exclusively
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Analyze Reaction 1 mechanism. The combination of a secondary alkyl halide, a strong nucleophile ($\text{OH}^-$), and a polar aprotic solvent (acetone) strongly favors the bimolecular $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ mechanism. The nucleophile attacks from the backside directly opposite to the departing bromide ion, resulting in clean Walden inversion from the $(R)$ configuration to the $(S)$ configuration.
Step 2: Analyze Reaction 2 mechanism. In the absence of a strong base and in the presence of a polar protic solvent mixture (water/ethanol), the substrate undergoes solvolysis via the unimolecular $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ mechanism. The rate-determining step forms a planar carbocation intermediate. Attack by water occurs on both faces of the planar carbocation, producing a racemic mixture.
Step 3: Understand ion-pair effect in $\text{S}_\text{N}1$. In practice, the departing leaving group temporarily shields the front face (intimate ion pair), leading to a slight excess of inversion over retention. Hence, Reaction 1 gives complete inversion, while Reaction 2 gives racemization with net partial inversion.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Which of the following represents the correct decreasing order of reactivity towards bimolecular nucleophilic substitution ($\text{S}_\text{N}2$) among the given primary and methyl alkyl bromides?
(I) Bromoethane
(II) Bromomethane
(III) 1-Bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane (neopentyl bromide)
(IV) 1-Bromobutane
options: A) $\text{I} > \text{II} > \text{IV} > \text{III}$
B) $\text{III} > \text{IV} > \text{I} > \text{II}$
C) $\text{II} > \text{IV} > \text{I} > \text{III}$
D) $\text{II} > \text{I} > \text{IV} > \text{III}$
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand factors controlling $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ reactivity. The rate of the $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ mechanism is primarily governed by steric hindrance at the carbon undergoing backside attack. Bulky alkyl groups directly on the $\alpha$-carbon or heavily substituted $\beta$-carbons shield the reaction center from the incoming nucleophile.
Step 2: Compare the substrates. Bromomethane ($\text{CH}_3\text{Br}$, II) has zero steric crowding and undergoes $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ displacement fastest. Bromoethane ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$, I) has one methyl group on the $\alpha$-carbon. 1-Bromobutane ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$, IV) has a longer propyl chain which offers slightly more steric hindrance than ethyl.
Step 3: Evaluate neopentyl bromide. In 1-bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane (neopentyl bromide, III), although the $\alpha$-carbon is primary, the $\beta$-carbon carries three bulky methyl groups. This tertiary butyl group severely blocks backside approach by the nucleophile, making neopentyl bromide virtually unreactive towards $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ (relative rate $\approx 10^{-5}$ compared to ethyl). Thus, the reactivity order is $\text{II} > \text{I} > \text{IV} > \text{III}$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Arrange the following halides in the correct decreasing order of their rates of hydrolysis via the $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ pathway:
(I) $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ (Benzyl chloride)
(II) $(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5)_2\text{CH-Cl}$ (Diphenylmethyl chloride)
(III) $(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5)_3\text{C-Cl}$ (Triphenylmethyl chloride)
(IV) $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$ (Chlorobenzene)
options: A) $\text{III} > \text{II} > \text{I} > \text{IV}$
B) $\text{IV} > \text{I} > \text{II} > \text{III}$
C) $\text{III} > \text{I} > \text{II} > \text{IV}$
D) $\text{II} > \text{III} > \text{I} > \text{IV}$
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand the rate-determining step in $\text{S}_\text{N}1$. The rate of the $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ reaction is determined by the stability of the intermediate carbocation formed during heterolysis of the carbon-halogen bond.
Step 2: Compare carbocation stabilities. 
- In triphenylmethyl chloride (III), the triphenylmethyl carbocation ($(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5)_3\text{C}^+$) is stabilized by extensive resonance across three aromatic rings (10 canonical forms).
- In diphenylmethyl chloride (II), the carbocation is stabilized by resonance across two aromatic rings (7 canonical forms).
- In benzyl chloride (I), the benzyl carbocation is stabilized by one aromatic ring (4 canonical forms).
- In chlorobenzene (IV), ionization would produce an extremely unstable phenyl cation with a localized vacant $sp^2$ orbital orthogonal to the $\pi$ system; chlorobenzene is practically inert towards $\text{S}_\text{N}1$.
Step 3: Conclude the decreasing order: $\text{III} > \text{II} > \text{I} > \text{IV}$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements regarding solvent effects on nucleophilic substitution reactions:
Statement I: The reaction of 1-bromobutane with sodium azide ($\text{NaN}_3$) proceeds substantially faster in dimethyl sulfoxide ($\text{DMSO}$) than in ethanol.
Statement II: Polar aprotic solvents selectively solvate cations through their dipole negative ends while leaving anions relatively naked and unencumbered, thereby increasing their nucleophilic reactivity.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer:
options: A) Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
B) Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
C) Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
D) Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Analyze Statement I. The reaction of 1-bromobutane (a primary halide) with azide ion ($\text{N}_3^-$) occurs via the bimolecular $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ mechanism. Polar aprotic solvents such as $\text{DMSO}$, $\text{DMF}$, and acetone accelerate $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ reactions by several orders of magnitude compared to protic solvents like ethanol. Statement I is correct.
Step 2: Analyze Statement II. Polar protic solvents (like ethanol or water) form strong hydrogen bonds with anions, surrounding them in a tight solvent shell that decreases their nucleophilicity. In contrast, polar aprotic solvents (like $\text{DMSO}$) lack hydrogen atoms bonded to electronegative elements; they efficiently coordinate to and solvate cations via the negative oxygen pole, but cannot hydrogen-bond to anions. Consequently, the nucleophilic anion remains 'naked' with high ground-state energy, significantly reducing the activation energy for $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ displacement. Statement II is correct.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Arrange the following chloroarenes in the correct increasing order of their reactivity towards nucleophilic aromatic substitution ($\text{S}_\text{N}\text{Ar}$) with aqueous sodium hydroxide:
(I) Chlorobenzene
(II) 4-Nitrochlorobenzene
(III) 2,4,6-Trinitrochlorobenzene
(IV) 2,4-Dinitrochlorobenzene
options: A) $\text{I} < \text{IV} < \text{II} < \text{III}$
B) $\text{III} < \text{IV} < \text{II} < \text{I}$
C) $\text{I} < \text{II} < \text{IV} < \text{III}$
D) $\text{II} < \text{I} < \text{IV} < \text{III}$
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand nucleophilic aromatic substitution ($\text{S}_\text{N}\text{Ar}$). The reaction proceeds via attack of the nucleophile on the carbon bearing halogen, forming a resonance-stabilized carbanion intermediate (Meisenheimer complex).
Step 2: Analyze the activating influence of nitro groups. Strongly electron-withdrawing nitro groups ($-\text{NO}_2$) placed at ortho and para positions delocalize and stabilize the developing negative charge through both strong inductive ($-I$) and resonance ($-R$) effects.
Step 3: Compare reaction conditions from NCERT:
- Chlorobenzene (I): requires drastic conditions ($623\text{ K}, 300\text{ atm}$, Dow process).
- 4-Nitrochlorobenzene (II): one $-p\text{-NO}_2$ group activates the ring; reacts with aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ at $443\text{ K}$.
- 2,4-Dinitrochlorobenzene (IV): two $-\text{NO}_2$ groups (ortho and para); reacts at $368\text{ K}$.
- 2,4,6-Trinitrochlorobenzene (picryl chloride, III): three $-\text{NO}_2$ groups; hydrolyzes merely upon warming with warm water.
Step 4: Conclude increasing order: $\text{I} < \text{II} < \text{IV} < \text{III}$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements regarding nucleophilic substitution of nitro-substituted haloarenes:
Statement I: The presence of a nitro group at the meta-position of chlorobenzene does not facilitate nucleophilic substitution to any significant extent compared to ortho- and para-positions.
Statement II: In the case of meta-nitrochlorobenzene, none of the resonating structures of the carbanion intermediate bears the negative charge on the ring carbon atom directly attached to the nitro group.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer:
options: A) Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
B) Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
C) Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
D) Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Evaluate Statement I. The presence of a nitro group at the meta-position has little activating effect on nucleophilic substitution because the intermediate carbanion cannot be stabilized by resonance with the meta-nitro group. Statement I is correct.
Step 2: Evaluate Statement II. During nucleophilic attack at the carbon bonded to chlorine in meta-nitrochlorobenzene, the canonical structures distribute negative charge over the ortho and para positions relative to the attack site. None of these resonance contributors places a negative formal charge on the carbon bearing the nitro group. Consequently, the powerful $-R$ resonance electron-withdrawing effect of the nitro group cannot stabilize the carbanion intermediate. In contrast, for ortho and para isomers, one resonance structure places the negative charge directly on the carbon bonded to $-\text{NO}_2$, enabling efficient delocalization into the oxygen atoms. Statement II is correct.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
When 2-bromo-2-methylbutane is treated separately with two different bases:
Base (X): Sodium ethoxide ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{O}^-\text{Na}^+$) in ethanol at $60^\circ\text{C}$
Base (Y): Potassium $tert$-butoxide ($(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CO}^-\text{K}^+$) in $tert$-butanol at $60^\circ\text{C}$
What are the predominant alkene products formed in reactions with Base (X) and Base (Y), respectively?
options: A) 2-Methylbut-2-ene with Base (X) and 2-Methylbut-1-ene with Base (Y)
B) 2-Methylbut-1-ene with Base (X) and 2-Methylbut-2-ene with Base (Y)
C) 2-Methylbut-2-ene with both Base (X) and Base (Y)
D) 2-Methylbut-1-ene with both Base (X) and Base (Y)
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the substrate structure. 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane is $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}(\text{Br})-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3$. It possesses two types of $\beta$-hydrogens: six equivalent primary $\beta$-hydrogens on the methyl carbons (C1), and two secondary $\beta$-hydrogens on the methylene carbon (C3).
Step 2: Analyze Base (X). Sodium ethoxide is a small, unhindered strong base. It abstracts the proton from the more substituted $\beta$-carbon (C3) according to Zaitsev's rule, yielding the more substituted, thermodynamically stable alkene: 2-methylbut-2-ene (trisubstituted alkene, stabilized by 9 hyperconjugative $\alpha$-hydrogens) as the major product.
Step 3: Analyze Base (Y). Potassium $tert$-butoxide is an extremely bulky base. Steric hindrance prevents it from easily abstracting a proton from the sterically congested internal methylene group (C3). Instead, it preferentially abstracts a more accessible, less hindered proton from the primary methyl groups (C1), yielding 2-methylbut-1-ene (disubstituted alkene, Hoffmann product) as the major product.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: When 2-bromo-2-methylpropane is treated with sodium ethoxide in ethanol, the major product is an alkene (P), but when heated in pure ethanol without sodium ethoxide, the major product is an ether (Q). Identify P and Q:
options: A) P = 2-Ethoxy-2-methylpropane, Q = 2-Methylpropene
B) P = 2-Methylpropene, Q = 2-Ethoxy-2-methylpropane ($tert$-butyl ethyl ether)
C) P = But-2-ene, Q = Diethyl ether
D) P = 2-Methylpropene, Q = Diethyl ether
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Analyze reaction with sodium ethoxide. Sodium ethoxide ($\text{EtO}^-$) is a powerful, unhindered base. When reacted with a tertiary alkyl halide (2-bromo-2-methylpropane), steric crowding completely suppresses $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ displacement. The strong base abstracts a $\beta$-proton via the E2 pathway to yield 2-methylpropene (isobutylene, P) as the exclusive major product.
Step 2: Analyze solvolysis in pure ethanol. Pure ethanol is a weak, neutral nucleophile and a weak base. Under these conditions, the tertiary alkyl halide undergoes unimolecular ionization ($\text{S}_\text{N}1$) to produce a stable tertiary carbocation ($(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^+$). Attack by ethanol followed by deprotonation yields $tert$-butyl ethyl ether (2-ethoxy-2-methylpropane, Q) as the major substitution product.
Step 3: Conclude the identities: P is 2-methylpropene and Q is 2-ethoxy-2-methylpropane.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Match the organic transformations and coupling reactions in List I with their corresponding named designations in List II:
List I:
(P) $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{NaI} \xrightarrow{\text{dry acetone}} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{I} + \text{NaBr}\downarrow$
(Q) $\text{CH}_3\text{Br} + \text{AgF} \xrightarrow{} \text{CH}_3\text{F} + \text{AgBr}$
(R) $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Br} + \text{CH}_3\text{Br} + 2\text{Na} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_3 + 2\text{NaBr}$
(S) $2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Br} + 2\text{Na} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{C}_6\text{H}_5 + 2\text{NaBr}$

List II:
(1) Fittig reaction
(2) Swarts reaction
(3) Wurtz-Fittig reaction
(4) Finkelstein reaction

Choose the correct match from the options below:
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Match reaction (P). The halogen exchange between an alkyl halide and $\text{NaI}$ in dry acetone is the Finkelstein reaction. Thus, $\text{P} \rightarrow 4$.
Step 2: Match reaction (Q). The conversion of an alkyl halide to an alkyl fluoride using a metallic fluoride like $\text{AgF}$ is the Swarts reaction. Thus, $\text{Q} \rightarrow 2$.
Step 3: Match reaction (R). The coupling of an aryl halide and an alkyl halide using sodium metal in dry ether to form an alkylarene is the Wurtz-Fittig reaction. Thus, $\text{R} \rightarrow 3$.
Step 4: Match reaction (S). The coupling of two aryl halide molecules using sodium in dry ether to yield a biaryl (biphenyl) is the Fittig reaction. Thus, $\text{S} \rightarrow 1$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: Free-radical photochemical bromination of 2-methylpropane with bromine ($\text{Br}_2/h\nu$) at $127^\circ\text{C}$ gives 2-bromo-2-methylpropane in greater than $99\%$ yield, whereas photochemical chlorination ($\text{Cl}_2/h\nu$) gives only $36\%$ of 2-chloro-2-methylpropane and $64\%$ of 1-chloro-2-methylpropane. The main reason for this dramatic difference in selectivity is that:
options: A) Bromine forms a cyclic bromonium ion with the alkane prior to substitution
B) Bromine radicals are smaller than chlorine radicals and can easily penetrate into crowded tertiary positions
C) Chlorine reacts exclusively by an ionic mechanism while bromine reacts by a radical mechanism

D) Hydrogen abstraction by bromine radical is endothermic and highly selective, with a transition state closely resembling the stable tertiary free radical, whereas chlorine radical abstraction is exothermic and non-selective
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Analyze thermodynamics of the hydrogen abstraction step. In free-radical halogenation, the hydrogen abstraction step ($\text{R}-\text{H} + \text{X}^\bullet \rightarrow \text{R}^\bullet + \text{H}-\text{X}$) determines regioselectivity. For chlorine, the step is exothermic ($\Delta H^\circ \approx -17\text{ kJ/mol}$), making the transition state early (resembling reactants according to Hammond's postulate); hence, chlorination is unselective and reactivity ratios ($1^\circ : 2^\circ : 3^\circ = 1 : 3.8 : 5.0$) are counterbalanced by the 9 primary hydrogens versus 1 tertiary hydrogen in 2-methylpropane.
Step 2: Analyze bromination selectivity. For bromine, hydrogen abstraction is endothermic ($\Delta H^\circ \approx +42\text{ kJ/mol}$). By Hammond's postulate, the transition state occurs late and resembles the radical intermediate, reflecting the energetic difference between tertiary and primary free radicals. The selectivity ratio of bromine is $1^\circ : 2^\circ : 3^\circ = 1 : 82 : 1600$.
Step 3: Conclude the reason: Bromination is highly selective for the tertiary position due to its endothermic nature and late transition state.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: When chlorobenzene undergoes nitration with a mixture of concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulfuric acid, 1-chloro-4-nitrobenzene is obtained as the major product ($70\%$) while 1-chloro-2-nitrobenzene is obtained as the minor product ($30\%$). The para-isomer dominates primarily because:
options: A) The para-position experiences significantly less steric hindrance between the incoming bulky nitronium group and the existing chlorine atom
B) The inductive electron-withdrawing effect of chlorine is completely absent at the para-position
C) The resonance electron-donating effect operates exclusively at the para-position and not at the ortho-position
D) Nitration at the ortho-position generates an anti-aromatic intermediate
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand directing influence of halogen. Chlorine possesses $+R$ resonance electron donation, which selectively increases electron density at both ortho and para positions relative to meta positions. Therefore, electrophilic nitration by the nitronium ion ($\text{NO}_2^+$) occurs at the ortho and para positions.
Step 2: Compare ortho vs para attack. The chlorine atom is a relatively large atom with high electron density. Attack of the electrophile at the adjacent ortho position experiences substantial steric repulsion and electrostatic clash with the chlorine substituent. In contrast, the para position is diametrically opposite and completely unhindered sterically.
Step 3: Conclude the product ratio: Due to minimal steric hindrance, the para-isomer (1-chloro-4-nitrobenzene) is formed as the major product ($70\%$).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: An alkyl halide $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{11}\text{Br}$ (Compound A) reacts with magnesium metal in dry ether to form a Grignard reagent (Compound B). When Compound B is treated with heavy water ($\text{D}_2\text{O}$), it gives 2-methylbutane-2-$d$ represented as $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C(D)}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3$. What is the IUPAC name of Compound A?
options: A) 1-Bromo-2-methylbutane
B) 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane
C) 2-Bromo-3-methylbutane
D) 1-Bromo-3-methylbutane
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Write the general Grignard reaction with heavy water: $\text{R}-\text{MgBr} + \text{D}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{R}-\text{D} + \text{Mg(OD)Br}$.
Step 2: Identify the position of deuterium. The product formed is $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C(D)}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3$, which has deuterium attached directly to carbon-2 of the 2-methylbutane skeleton.
Step 3: Deduce the alkyl group. The carbon atom attached to deuterium (C2) must be the exact carbon that was bonded to magnesium in the Grignard reagent, which in turn was the carbon bonded to bromine in Compound A. Thus, Compound A must be 2-bromo-2-methylbutane.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements labeled as Assertion (A) and Reason (R):
Assertion (A): Allyl chloride ($\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$) undergoes nucleophilic substitution reactions much more readily than vinyl chloride ($\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-\text{Cl}$).
Reason (R): In allyl chloride, heterolytic cleavage of the $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond yields a carbocation stabilized by resonance across the adjacent double bond, whereas in vinyl chloride, the $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond has partial double bond character due to resonance and the vinylic cation is highly unstable.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer:
options: A) (A) is true but (R) is false
B) Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
C) Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
D) (A) is false but (R) is true
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Evaluate Assertion (A). Allyl chloride readily undergoes both $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ and $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ nucleophilic substitution reactions, whereas vinyl chloride is exceptionally inert towards nucleophiles. Assertion (A) is true.
Step 2: Evaluate Reason (R). In allyl chloride, ionization gives the allyl carbocation ($[\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2^+ \leftrightarrow ^+\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2]$), which is stabilized by resonance between two equivalent structures. In vinyl chloride, the unshared electron pair of chlorine is conjugated with the double bond ($[\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-\text{Cl} \leftrightarrow ^-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}=\text{Cl}^+]$), giving partial double bond character and shortening the bond. Moreover, cleavage of vinyl chloride would produce a vinyl carbocation where the positive charge is localized in an $sp$ orbital, which is energetically very unfavorable. Reason (R) is true and correctly explains Assertion (A).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: How many monochloro derivatives (including stereoisomers) are theoretically possible from the photochemical free-radical monochlorination of 2-methylbutane?
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify all constitutionally isomeric monochloro derivatives of 2-methylbutane ($\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3$):
1. 1-Chloro-2-methylbutane: $\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3$
2. 2-Chloro-2-methylbutane: $\text{CH}_3-\text{C(Cl)}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3$
3. 2-Chloro-3-methylbutane: $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH(Cl)}-\text{CH}_3$
4. 1-Chloro-3-methylbutane: $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$
Step 2: Determine chirality for each isomer:
- In 1-chloro-2-methylbutane, C2 is bonded to $-\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$, $-\text{H}$, $-\text{CH}_3$, and $-\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$. It is a chiral center, giving a pair of enantiomers ($2$ stereoisomers: $R$ and $S$).
- In 2-chloro-2-methylbutane, C2 has two identical methyl groups; it is achiral ($1$ isomer).
- In 2-chloro-3-methylbutane, C2 is bonded to $-\text{H}$, $-\text{Cl}$, $-\text{CH}_3$, and an isopropyl group. It has a chiral center, giving a pair of enantiomers ($2$ stereoisomers: $R$ and $S$).
- In 1-chloro-3-methylbutane, no carbon has four different groups; it is achiral ($1$ isomer).
Step 3: Sum total stereoisomers: $2 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 6$ stereoisomers.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements regarding chlorofluorocarbons (Freons):
(I) Freon-12 (dichlorodifluoromethane, $\text{CCl}_2\text{F}_2$) is manufactured industrially from tetrachloromethane by the Swarts reaction using antimony trifluoride in the presence of antimony pentachloride.
(II) Freons are extremely stable, unreactive, non-toxic, non-corrosive, and easily liquefiable gases.
(III) In the stratosphere, Freon-12 undergoes photochemical homolysis by ultraviolet radiation to release chlorine free radicals that catalytically destroy ozone molecules.
Which of the above statements are correct according to NCERT?
options: A) (I), (II), and (III)
B) (I) and (II) only
C) (II) and (III) only
D) (I) and (III) only
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Evaluate statement (I). Freon-12 ($\text{CCl}_2\text{F}_2$) is one of the most common chlorofluorocarbons and is manufactured from $\text{CCl}_4$ by the Swarts reaction: $3\text{CCl}_4 + 2\text{SbF}_3 \xrightarrow{\text{SbCl}_5} 3\text{CCl}_2\text{F}_2 + 2\text{SbCl}_3$. Statement (I) is correct.
Step 2: Evaluate statement (II). NCERT explicitly describes Freons as extremely stable, unreactive, non-toxic, non-corrosive, and easily liquefiable gases, which led to their widespread use as refrigerants and aerosol propellants. Statement (II) is correct.
Step 3: Evaluate statement (III). In the stratosphere, intense UV radiation initiates homolytic fission of $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bonds in freons: $\text{CF}_2\text{Cl}_2 \xrightarrow{h\nu} ^\bullet\text{CF}_2\text{Cl} + \text{Cl}^\bullet$. The chlorine radical reacts with ozone: $\text{Cl}^\bullet + \text{O}_3 \rightarrow \text{ClO}^\bullet + \text{O}_2$, and $\text{ClO}^\bullet + \text{O} \rightarrow \text{Cl}^\bullet + \text{O}_2$. A single chlorine radical can destroy up to $100{,}000$ ozone molecules. Statement (III) is correct.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Consider the following reaction sequence:
$\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{HBr, benzoyl peroxide}} \text{Compound A} \xrightarrow{\text{AgCN (alc.)}} \text{Compound B} \xrightarrow{\text{LiAlH}_4} \text{Compound C}$
What is the correct IUPAC name of Compound C?
options: A) Butan-1-amine
B) $N$-Methylpropan-1-amine
C) $N,N$-Dimethylpropan-1-amine
D) 2-Methylpropan-1-amine
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify Compound A. Addition of $\text{HBr}$ to propene in the presence of benzoyl peroxide proceeds via the anti-Markovnikov free-radical pathway to give 1-bromopropane: $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$.
Step 2: Identify Compound B. Reaction of 1-bromopropane with silver cyanide ($\text{AgCN}$), a covalent reagent, results in nucleophilic attack through the lone pair of the nitrogen atom to form an alkyl isocyanide: propyl isocyanide ($\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{NC}$).
Step 3: Identify Compound C. Reduction of an alkyl isocyanide with lithium aluminium hydride ($\text{LiAlH}_4$) reduces the isonitrile group into a secondary amine containing an $N$-methyl group: $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{NH}-\text{CH}_3$. The IUPAC name is $N$-methylpropan-1-amine.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: Which of the following haloalkanes, upon alkaline hydrolysis with aqueous sodium hydroxide followed by treatment with iodine ($\text{I}_2$) in alkaline medium, produces a yellow precipitate of triiodomethane (iodoform)?
options: A) 3-Chloropentane
B) 1-Chlorobutane
C) 2-Chlorobutane
D) 1-Chloropropane
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand the iodoform test requirement. The haloform/iodoform reaction requires compounds containing either the $\text{CH}_3-\text{C}=\text{O}$ group or the $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH(OH)}-$ group, which can be oxidized by hypoiodite ($\text{OI}^-$) to a methyl ketone.
Step 2: Determine the hydrolysis product of each haloalkane:
- Alkaline hydrolysis of 2-chlorobutane gives butan-2-ol ($\text{CH}_3-\text{CH(OH)}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3$), which contains the $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH(OH)}-$ unit.
- Alkaline hydrolysis of 1-chlorobutane gives butan-1-ol (primary alcohol, no $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH(OH)}-$ unit).
- Alkaline hydrolysis of 3-chloropentane gives pentan-3-ol ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2-\text{CH(OH)}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, no methyl group directly attached to the carbinol carbon).
- Alkaline hydrolysis of 1-chloropropane gives propan-1-ol (primary alcohol).
Step 3: Conclude the positive test: Butan-2-ol from 2-chlorobutane is oxidized to butan-2-one and then iodinated and cleaved to form a yellow crystalline precipitate of iodoform ($\text{CHI}_3$).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements regarding the organochlorine insecticide DDT ($p,p'$-dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane):
Statement I: DDT is prepared commercially by the condensation of chloral (trichloroethanal, $\text{CCl}_3\text{CHO}$) with chlorobenzene in the presence of concentrated sulfuric acid.
Statement II: DDT is highly water-soluble and rapidly metabolized and excreted by animals, which is why it poses no bioaccumulation hazards.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer:
options: A) Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
B) Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
C) Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
D) Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Evaluate Statement I. DDT is synthesized by condensing one molecule of chloral with two molecules of chlorobenzene in the presence of concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ as a dehydrating agent: $\text{CCl}_3\text{CHO} + 2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Cl} \xrightarrow{\text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4} (p\text{-Cl}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4)_2\text{CH}-\text{CCl}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. Statement I is correct.
Step 2: Evaluate Statement II. DDT has extremely low water solubility and high lipid solubility. Because of its chemical stability and lipid affinity, it is not rapidly metabolized or excreted; instead, it accumulates in the fatty tissues of animals. This leads to biomagnification along food chains, causing serious reproductive and ecological damage (such as eggshell thinning in birds of prey), leading to its global ban. Statement II is incorrect.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Match the inorganic reagents reacting with haloalkane ($\text{R}-\text{X}$) in List I with the primary functional group class of the organic product in List II:
List I:
(P) $\text{KCN}$ in aqueous alcohol
(Q) $\text{AgCN}$ in aqueous alcohol
(R) $\text{KNO}_2$ in aqueous alcohol
(S) $\text{AgNO}_2$ in aqueous alcohol

List II:
(1) Nitroalkane ($\text{R}-\text{NO}_2$)
(2) Alkyl isocyanide (carbylamine, $\text{R}-\text{NC}$)
(3) Alkyl nitrite ($\text{R}-\text{O}-\text{N}=\text{O}$)
(4) Alkyl cyanide (nitrile, $\text{R}-\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$)

Choose the correct match from the options below:
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Match (P) $\text{KCN}$. $\text{KCN}$ is ionic and provides cyanide ion ($[:\text{C}\equiv\text{N}:]^-$). Attack occurs predominantly through carbon to yield an alkyl cyanide (nitrile, $\text{R}-\text{CN}$). Thus, $\text{P} \rightarrow 4$.
Step 2: Match (Q) $\text{AgCN}$. $\text{AgCN}$ is covalent and attack takes place through the lone pair of electrons on nitrogen, yielding an alkyl isocyanide (isocyanide, $\text{R}-\text{NC}$). Thus, $\text{Q} \rightarrow 2$.
Step 3: Match (R) $\text{KNO}_2$. $\text{KNO}_2$ is ionic and provides nitrite ion ($[\text{O}-\text{N}=\text{O}]^-$). The negative charge on oxygen attacks the alkyl carbon, producing an alkyl nitrite ($\text{R}-\text{O}-\text{N}=\text{O}$). Thus, $\text{R} \rightarrow 3$.
Step 4: Match (S) $\text{AgNO}_2$. $\text{AgNO}_2$ is predominantly covalent; the nitrogen lone pair attacks the alkyl carbon, resulting in a nitroalkane ($\text{R}-\text{NO}_2$). Thus, $\text{S} \rightarrow 1$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: When 2-bromo-3,3-dimethylbutane is heated with aqueous ethanol in the absence of a strong base, the major solvolysis substitution product obtained is:
options: A) 2-Ethoxy-3,3-dimethylbutane
B) 2-Ethoxy-2,3-dimethylbutane
C) 3,3-Dimethylbutan-2-ol
D) 1-Ethoxy-3,3-dimethylbutane
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the mechanism. Heating with a neutral polar protic solvent (aqueous ethanol) without a strong base promotes solvolysis via the unimolecular $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ pathway.
Step 2: Trace carbocation formation and rearrangement. Heterolytic departure of the bromide ion from 2-bromo-3,3-dimethylbutane ($(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{CH(Br)}-\text{CH}_3$) generates an initial secondary carbocation: $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{CH}^+-\text{CH}_3$. To relieve angle strain and achieve greater electronic stability, a 1,2-methyl shift occurs from the adjacent quaternary carbon. This transforms the less stable secondary carbocation into a significantly more stable tertiary carbocation: $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}^+-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$.
Step 3: Determine the product. Nucleophilic capture of this rearranged tertiary carbocation by ethanol ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$) followed by proton loss produces 2-ethoxy-2,3-dimethylbutane as the predominant substitution product.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: In bimolecular $\text{E}2$ dehydrohalogenation reactions, elimination requires an anti-periplanar conformation between the $\beta$-hydrogen and the leaving halogen. Treatment of $(1R,2S)$-1-chloro-1,2-diphenylpropane with sodium ethoxide in ethanol predominantly yields:
options: A) 3,3-Diphenylprop-1-ene
B) $(E)$-1,2-Diphenylprop-1-ene
C) $(Z)$-1,2-Diphenylprop-1-ene
D) 1,2-Diphenylprop-2-ene
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand the stereoelectronic requirement of the $\text{E}2$ mechanism. For orbital overlap to smoothly convert $sp^3$ hybrid orbitals into the newly forming $\pi$ bond, the $\text{C}_\beta-\text{H}$ bond and the $\text{C}_\alpha-\text{Cl}$ bond must lie in the same plane and point in opposite directions (dihedral angle $= 180^\circ$, anti-periplanar conformation).
Step 2: Draw the Newman projection for $(1R,2S)$-1-chloro-1,2-diphenylpropane. On C1 (front), we have $-\text{Cl}$, $-\text{H}$, and $-\text{C}_6\text{H}_5$. On C2 (back), we have $-\text{H}$, $-\text{CH}_3$, and $-\text{C}_6\text{H}_5$. Rotating about the $\text{C}_1-\text{C}_2$ single bond to place the $\beta$-hydrogen exactly anti to the leaving chlorine group puts the two bulky phenyl ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5$) rings on the same side of the developing double bond.
Step 3: Conclude the alkene geometry. Simultaneous abstraction of the anti-hydrogen by ethoxide and loss of chloride locks the geometry into $(Z)$-1,2-diphenylprop-1-ene as the major stereospecific elimination product.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: The bridgehead halide 1-bromobicyclo[2.2.1]heptane is exceptionally inert towards both $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ and $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ nucleophilic substitutions. Which of the following provides the correct mechanistic justification?
options: A) The bridgehead carbon is $sp$-hybridized and cannot accommodate incoming electron pairs
B) The carbon-bromine bond has $100\%$ ionic character which prevents nucleophilic displacement
C) The bicyclic cage easily undergoes ring expansion to form an unreactive cyclobutane derivative
D) Inability of the bridgehead carbon to adopt a planar $sp^2$ geometry prevents carbocation formation (Bredt's rule), while the cage structure rigidly blocks backside attack by nucleophiles
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Analyze resistance to the $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ pathway. Ionization via $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ requires the bridgehead carbon to become a carbocation. A stable carbocation must attain planar $sp^2$ geometry (bond angles $120^\circ$). In the rigid bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane cage, the bridgehead carbon is constrained to a pyramidal geometry with bond angles constrained near $109.5^\circ$ or smaller, creating intolerable ring strain that forbids planarity. Furthermore, according to Bredt's rule, a bridgehead double bond or planar radical/cation cannot be accommodated in small bicyclic rings.
Step 2: Analyze resistance to the $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ pathway. The $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ mechanism requires backside attack at $180^\circ$ relative to the carbon-bromine bond. The rigid bicyclic carbon framework encloses the backside of the bridgehead carbon, making it sterically impossible for any nucleophile to access the reaction center from behind.
Step 3: Conclude why both pathways fail: Bridgehead geometry forbids both planarity for $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ and backside approach for $\text{S}_\text{N}2$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Consider the following multi-step reaction cascade:
$\text{Toluene} \xrightarrow{3\text{Cl}_2/h\nu, \Delta} \text{Compound A} \xrightarrow{\text{aq. Ca(OH)}_2, \Delta} \text{Compound B} \xrightarrow{\text{PCl}_5} \text{Compound C} \xrightarrow{\text{H}_2, \text{Pd-BaSO}_4, \text{quinoline}} \text{Compound D}$
What is the IUPAC name and structure of Compound D?
options: A) Benzaldehyde ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CHO}$)
B) Benzyl alcohol ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$)
C) Acetophenone ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCH}_3$)
D) Benzoic acid ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}$)
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify Compound A. Photochemical chlorination of boiling toluene with excess chlorine ($3\text{Cl}_2/h\nu$) results in complete free-radical chlorination of the benzylic methyl group to form benzotrichloride: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CCl}_3$.
Step 2: Identify Compound B. Hydrolysis of benzotrichloride with aqueous base ($(\text{aq. Ca(OH)}_2)$ or $\text{aq. NaOH}$) replaces the three chlorine atoms with three $-\text{OH}$ groups on the same carbon, which spontaneously loses water to produce benzoic acid: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}$.
Step 3: Identify Compound C. Treatment of benzoic acid with $\text{PCl}_5$ yields benzoyl chloride: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCl} + \text{POCl}_3 + \text{HCl}$.
Step 4: Identify Compound D. Catalytic hydrogenation of benzoyl chloride using Lindlar-type Rosenmund catalyst ($\text{H}_2$ over $\text{Pd-BaSO}_4$ poisoned with quinoline or sulfur) selectively reduces the acid chloride to benzaldehyde ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CHO}$).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
The nucleophilic substitution of a secondary alkyl halide $\text{R}-\text{Br}$ in aqueous ethanol proceeds concurrently through both unimolecular and bimolecular pathways according to the total rate law:
$$\text{Rate} = k_1[\text{RBr}] + k_2[\text{RBr}][\text{OH}^-]$$
At initial concentrations $[\text{RBr}] = 0.10\text{ M}$ and $[\text{OH}^-] = 0.10\text{ M}$, the $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ pathway accounts for $40\%$ of the total substitution while the $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ pathway accounts for $60\%$. If $[\text{RBr}]$ is doubled to $0.20\text{ M}$ and $[\text{OH}^-]$ is quadrupled to $0.40\text{ M}$, by what factor does the total rate of reaction increase?
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Set up the initial rate expressions. Let the initial total rate be $R_0 = 100\text{ units}$.
The initial $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ component is $R_{1,0} = k_1[\text{RBr}]_0 = 40\text{ units}$.
The initial $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ component is $R_{2,0} = k_2[\text{RBr}]_0[\text{OH}^-]_0 = 60\text{ units}$.
Step 2: Determine new rates under altered concentrations. $[\text{RBr}] = 2[\text{RBr}]_0$ and $[\text{OH}^-] = 4[\text{OH}^-]_0$.
- For the $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ pathway (first-order in $[\text{RBr}]$, independent of $[\text{OH}^-]$):
$$R_{1,\text{new}} = k_1(2[\text{RBr}]_0) = 2 \times R_{1,0} = 2 \times 40 = 80\text{ units}$$
- For the $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ pathway (first-order in $[\text{RBr}]$ and first-order in $[\text{OH}^-]$):
$$R_{2,\text{new}} = k_2(2[\text{RBr}]_0)(4[\text{OH}^-]_0) = 8 \times R_{2,0} = 8 \times 60 = 480\text{ units}$$
Step 3: Calculate the new total rate and fold change:
$$R_{\text{total, new}} = R_{1,\text{new}} + R_{2,\text{new}} = 80 + 480 = 560\text{ units}$$
$$\text{Factor increase} = \frac{R_{\text{total, new}}}{R_0} = \frac{560}{100} = 5.6$$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements regarding nucleophilic aromatic substitution ($\text{S}_\text{N}\text{Ar}$) of activated haloarenes:
Statement I: In the reaction of 1-halo-2,4-dinitrobenzenes with amines, 1-fluoro-2,4-dinitrobenzene reacts dramatically faster than 1-chloro- or 1-bromo-2,4-dinitrobenzene ($-\text{F} \gg -\text{Cl} \approx -\text{Br} \approx -\text{I}$).
Statement II: In the $\text{S}_\text{N}\text{Ar}$ addition-elimination mechanism, the rate-determining step is the nucleophilic addition to form the Meisenheimer intermediate; the high electronegativity of fluorine strongly stabilizes the negative charge in the transition state, whereas the subsequent loss of halide is fast.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer:
options: A) Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
B) Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
C) Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
D) Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Evaluate Statement I. Sanger's reagent (1-fluoro-2,4-dinitrobenzene) reacts with amino groups hundreds of times faster than 1-chloro-2,4-dinitrobenzene ($-\text{F} \gg -\text{Cl} \approx -\text{Br}$). This is opposite to aliphatic nucleophilic substitutions where fluoride is the worst leaving group. Statement I is correct.
Step 2: Evaluate Statement II. The $\text{S}_\text{N}\text{Ar}$ mechanism consists of two steps: Step 1 is the addition of the nucleophile to form a cyclohexadienyl anion (Meisenheimer complex), and Step 2 is the expulsion of the halide leaving group. Because aromaticity is lost in Step 1, Step 1 has a high activation barrier and is the slow, rate-determining step. Due to its superior electronegativity, fluorine withdraws electron density most strongly via induction ($-I$), lowering the activation energy for the nucleophile's attack and heavily stabilizing the carbanionic transition state. Carbon-halogen bond cleavage occurs in the second, fast step; hence leaving group ability does not dictate the overall rate. Statement II is correct.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Consider the following chemical reactions performed on optically pure $(S)$-2-bromobutane:
(I) Reaction with sodium iodide ($\text{NaI}$) in dry acetone yielding 2-iodobutane.
(II) Reaction with sodium hydrosulfide ($\text{NaSH}$) in ethanol yielding butan-2-thiol.
(III) Reaction with alcoholic potassium hydroxide ($\text{alc. KOH}$) at elevated temperature yielding but-2-ene.
(IV) Reaction with magnesium in dry ether followed by treatment with water yielding butane.
Which of the following statements correctly identifies the stereochemical outcome of these transformations?
options: A) Reaction (III) yields an optically active $(Z)$-alkene as the major product
B) All four reactions yield products that retain the $(S)$ configuration and remain optically active
C) Reaction (I) yields a racemic mixture while Reaction (II) gives retention of configuration
D) Reactions (I) and (II) proceed with complete inversion of configuration at the stereocenter, while reactions (III) and (IV) yield optically inactive products
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Analyze Reaction (I). The Finkelstein reaction of $(S)$-2-bromobutane with $\text{NaI}$ in acetone follows a bimolecular $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ mechanism involving backside attack. This leads to complete inversion of configuration, forming $(R)$-2-iodobutane.
Step 2: Analyze Reaction (II). Similarly, the hydrosulfide anion ($\text{SH}^-$) is a powerful, compact nucleophile that displaces bromide via $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ with complete inversion of configuration, forming $(R)$-butan-2-thiol.
Step 3: Analyze Reaction (III). $\beta$-Elimination by alcoholic $\text{KOH}$ predominantly yields but-2-ene ($\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_3$). But-2-ene lacks an asymmetric carbon and has a plane of symmetry, making it achiral and optically inactive.
Step 4: Analyze Reaction (IV). Formation of the Grignard reagent followed by protonation gives butane ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$), which is achiral and optically inactive. Thus, (I) and (II) invert configuration, whereas (III) and (IV) yield optically inactive products.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements labeled as Assertion (A) and Reason (R):
Assertion (A): Chlorobenzene does not produce any precipitate of silver chloride ($\text{AgCl}$) when warmed with aqueous silver nitrate solution, whereas benzyl chloride produces an immediate curdy white precipitate.
Reason (R): In chlorobenzene, delocalization of chlorine lone pairs gives the $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond partial double bond character and suppresses ionization, whereas benzyl chloride readily ionizes to form a resonance-stabilized benzyl carbocation.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer:
options: A) Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
B) Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
C) (A) is true but (R) is false
D) (A) is false but (R) is true
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Evaluate Assertion (A). Treatment with ethanolic or aqueous $\text{AgNO}_3$ is a diagnostic test for ionizable halide ions. Chlorobenzene does not react with $\text{AgNO}_3$ even upon heating, while benzyl chloride forms a white precipitate of $\text{AgCl}$ rapidly. Assertion (A) is true.
Step 2: Evaluate Reason (R). In benzyl chloride ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$), the chlorine is attached to an $sp^3$ benzylic carbon. Heterolytic cleavage is assisted by $\text{Ag}^+$ precipitation to give a benzyl carbocation ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2^+$), which is strongly stabilized by resonance across the aromatic ring. In contrast, in chlorobenzene, the chlorine lone pairs are delocalized into the $\pi$ system ($+R$ resonance), imparting partial double bond character to the $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond and making it shorter and much stronger ($169\text{ pm}$ vs $178\text{ pm}$). Furthermore, self-ionization would generate an extremely unstable phenyl cation with a localized vacant $sp^2$ orbital orthogonal to the $\pi$ cloud. Thus, Reason (R) is true and correctly explains Assertion (A).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
Match the reaction sequences involving haloalkanes or haloarenes in List I with their corresponding major organic products in List II:
List I:
(P) $\text{Benzene} + \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl} \xrightarrow{\text{anhyd. AlCl}_3} \text{Product}$
(Q) $\text{Phenol} + \text{CHCl}_3 + 3\text{NaOH} \xrightarrow{340\text{ K}} \xrightarrow{\text{H}^+} \text{Product}$
(R) $\text{Chlorobenzene} + \text{CH}_3\text{Cl} + 2\text{Na} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \text{Product}$
(S) $\text{Aniline} \xrightarrow{\text{NaNO}_2 + \text{HCl}, 273-278\text{ K}} \xrightarrow{\text{Cu}_2\text{Cl}_2/\text{HCl}} \text{Product}$

List II:
(1) Chlorobenzene
(2) Toluene
(3) Salicylaldehyde
(4) Isopropylbenzene (cumene)

Choose the correct match from the options below:
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Match reaction (P). Friedel-Crafts alkylation of benzene with 1-chloropropane in the presence of $\text{anhyd. AlCl}_3$ generates a primary propyl carbocation, which rapidly undergoes a 1,2-hydride shift to form the more stable secondary isopropyl carbocation. Electrophilic aromatic attack by this carbocation on benzene gives isopropylbenzene (cumene) as the major product. Thus, $\text{P} \rightarrow 4$.
Step 2: Match reaction (Q). Treatment of phenol with chloroform and aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ at $340\text{ K}$ followed by acidification is the Reimer-Tiemann reaction, generating dichlorocarbene (:$!\text{CCl}_2$) as the electrophile to yield salicylaldehyde (2-hydroxybenzaldehyde). Thus, $\text{Q} \rightarrow 3$.
Step 3: Match reaction (R). Coupling of an aryl halide (chlorobenzene) and an alkyl halide (chloromethane) with sodium in dry ether is the Wurtz-Fittig reaction, producing toluene (methylbenzene). Thus, $\text{R} \rightarrow 2$.
